title: Presumptive Taxation for Non-Specified Businesses & Delivery Fleets (Section 44AD)
content: Gig workers operating as delivery fleet partners, contractors, or small business operators who do not fall under specified professions can declare net income at 6% of digital turnover (or 8% for cash) under Section 44AD, up to a turnover ceiling of ₹3 Crores (provided cash receipts do not exceed 5%).

title: Single Installment Advance Tax for Presumptive Taxation (Section 211)
content: Freelancers and gig workers opting for presumptive taxation under Section 44ADA or 44AD are exempt from the standard 4-installment advance tax schedule. They are only required to pay 100% of their estimated advance tax liability in a single installment on or before March 15 of the financial year.

title: Depreciation on Laptops, Workstation & Hardware (Section 32)
content: Freelancers filing under the regular tax scheme (non-presumptive) can claim annual depreciation on capitalized business assets: 40% on laptops, desktops, and computer software; 15% on office furniture and general equipment used for client deliverables.

title: Software Subscriptions, Cloud Hosting & Tooling (Section 37)
content: Monthly and annual subscription costs for specialized professional software (e.g., Adobe Creative Cloud, Figma, GitHub, Jira), cloud computing/servers (AWS, Google Cloud), and domain hosting used to produce client work are 100% tax-deductible under Section 37(1).

title: Coworking Space Fees & Home Office Rent (Section 37)
content: Freelancers can deduct 100% of commercial coworking desk rentals and meeting room charges. Those operating out of rented residential property can claim a proportionate share of rent and electricity attributable specifically to their dedicated workspace.

title: TDS Deductions by Indian Clients on Professional Fees (Section 194J)
content: Indian corporate and business clients deduct 10% (or 2% for technical/BPO services) TDS under Section 194J on aggregate annual payouts exceeding ₹30,000. Freelancers can offset this withheld amount directly against their net annual income tax liability using Form 26AS and AIS.

title: TDS on Contractual Work & Event Subcontracting (Section 194C)
content: Clients hiring gig workers for contract-based jobs (such as event photography, logistics, or content production) deduct 1% TDS for individual contractors on single payments over ₹30,000 or aggregate annual payments exceeding ₹1,00,000, claimable as a tax credit on filing.

title: Mandatory GST Registration Threshold for Service Providers (Section 22)
content: Gig workers and freelancers providing domestic services must register for GST once their aggregate turnover exceeds ₹20 Lakhs in a financial year (₹10 Lakhs for Special Category States). Below this threshold, registration remains optional.

title: Zero-Rated Export of Services via Letter of Undertaking (LUT)
content: Freelancers registered under GST who deliver services to international clients and receive payment in convertible foreign exchange qualify for zero-rated export. By filing an annual Letter of Undertaking (LUT / Form GST RFD-11), they can invoice overseas clients at 0% GST without paying upfront 18% IGST.

title: Mandatory FIRC / e-FIRA for Foreign Remittances
content: Freelancers earning foreign income via wire transfers, Stripe, PayPal, or Wise must secure a Foreign Inward Remittance Advice (e-FIRA/FIRC) from their Authorized Dealer bank. This document serves as statutory proof of export under RBI FEMA regulations and GST zero-rating audits.

title: Income Tax Return Form Selection (ITR-4 vs ITR-3)
content: Freelancers and gig workers opting for presumptive taxation under Section 44ADA or 44AD must file Form ITR-4 (Sugam). Those declaring actual profit and loss, claiming detailed itemized business expenses, carrying forward losses, or earning above presumptive turnover caps must file Form ITR-3.

title: Maintenance of Books of Accounts Requirement (Section 44AA)
content: Specified professionals filing under the regular tax scheme (non-presumptive) must formally maintain books of accounts (cash books, journals, ledgers, and expense bills) if their gross professional income exceeds ₹1.5 Lakhs in any of the 3 preceding financial years.

title: Mandatory Tax Audit Thresholds (Section 44AB)
content: A tax audit by a Chartered Accountant is mandatory under Section 44AB if professional gross receipts exceed ₹50 Lakhs (or ₹75 Lakhs if cash is ≤5%) and declared net profit is below 50%, or if business turnover exceeds ₹10 Crores (where digital receipts are ≥95%).

title: Foreign Assets and Overseas Account Disclosures (Schedule FA)
content: Freelancers maintaining foreign bank accounts, foreign currency wallets (like offshore PayPal balances), or holding equity/RSUs in foreign client firms must disclose them under Schedule FA in Form ITR-3 to avoid severe non-disclosure penalties under the Black Money Act.

title: Subcontractor Payouts & TDS Compliance Disallowance (Section 40(a)(ia))
content: Freelancers who outsource tasks to other contractors can claim those payments as legitimate deductible business expenses under Section 37, provided they deduct and remit applicable TDS under Section 194C or 194J. Failure to deduct TDS results in a 30% disallowance of the expense under Section 40(a)(ia).

title: Fuel Expenses Deduction for Ride-Hailing & Cab Drivers (Section 37)
content: Cab drivers and ride-hailing partners (Uber, Ola, Rapido) operating under the regular tax scheme (not presumptive) can claim 100% of petrol, diesel, or CNG fuel costs incurred exclusively for transporting passengers as a business expense under Section 37(1). Valid fuel receipts from petrol pumps (HPCL, BPCL, IOC, Indian Oil) must be preserved as documentary evidence. Fuel for personal use must be excluded. For drivers opting for presumptive taxation under Section 44AE or 44AD, fuel costs are automatically subsumed within the presumptive profit calculation and cannot be separately claimed.

title: Vehicle Maintenance, Servicing & Repair Deduction for Cab Drivers (Section 37)
content: Ride-hailing drivers filing under the regular tax scheme can fully deduct all vehicle maintenance and repair costs directly related to their taxi business under Section 37(1). This includes annual car servicing charges, engine oil and filter changes, tyre replacement, brake servicing, periodic pollution-under-control (PUC) checks, and any mechanical or electrical repair bills. The vehicle must be registered as a commercial vehicle or used exclusively/predominantly for earning income. Drivers opting for Section 44AE presumptive taxation cannot separately claim these costs as they are deemed included in the flat-rate deemed profit.

title: Mobile Recharge & Internet Expense for Ride-Hailing App Usage (Section 37)
content: Cab and delivery gig workers who use mobile internet connectivity to receive and navigate ride or delivery assignments through apps like Uber, Ola, Swiggy, or Zomato can claim their monthly mobile recharge, SIM data plan, and high-speed internet bill as a 100% deductible business expense under Section 37(1). If the same mobile connection is used partially for personal use, only the business-use proportion (typically 80-100% for full-time gig drivers) is deductible. Documentary evidence in the form of operator bills or recharge receipts must be maintained.

title: Vehicle Depreciation for Cab & Commercial Transport Operators (Section 32)
content: Ride-hailing cab drivers and transport operators who own their vehicle and file under the regular tax scheme can claim annual depreciation on the vehicle as a deductible expense under Section 32. The depreciation rate for motor cars used in a taxi business is 30% on Written Down Value (WDV). If the vehicle is purchased and put to use for less than 180 days in the financial year, only 50% of the normal depreciation (i.e., 15%) is allowed for that year. Drivers under presumptive Section 44AE cannot separately claim depreciation as it is already factored into the deemed income.

title: Presumptive Taxation for Goods Carriage & Commercial Vehicle Owners (Section 44AE)
content: Cab drivers and commercial vehicle operators owning up to 10 goods carriages at any time during the financial year can opt for presumptive taxation under Section 44AE. Deemed profit is calculated as ₹1,000 per tonne of gross vehicle weight (or unladen weight for light vehicles) per month or part of a month for which the vehicle is owned. Under 44AE, no separate deduction for fuel, maintenance, insurance, driver salary, or depreciation is permitted as all such expenses are deemed subsumed. Eligible taxpayers file Form ITR-4 (Sugam) and are exempt from maintaining detailed books of accounts.

title: Income Tax Slabs under New Tax Regime (FY 2024-25 / AY 2025-26)
content: Under the New Tax Regime (default from FY 2023-24 onwards, Section 115BAC), income tax for individuals is levied at the following progressive slab rates for FY 2024-25 (AY 2025-26): (1) Up to ₹3,00,000 — Nil (0%); (2) ₹3,00,001 to ₹7,00,000 — 5%; (3) ₹7,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 — 10%; (4) ₹10,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 — 15%; (5) ₹12,00,001 to ₹15,00,000 — 20%; (6) Above ₹15,00,000 — 30%. A standard deduction of ₹75,000 is available to salaried individuals and pensioners under the new regime. No HRA, LTA, 80C, 80D, or most other Chapter VI-A deductions are permitted. Gig workers and freelancers with no salary income cannot claim the standard deduction. A Section 87A tax rebate of up to ₹25,000 is available if total taxable income does not exceed ₹7,00,000, making the effective tax liability zero for incomes up to ₹7 Lakhs. A 4% Health and Education Cess is applied on the final tax amount. Surcharge applies at 10% (income ₹50L–₹1Cr), 15% (₹1Cr–₹2Cr), 25% (₹2Cr–₹5Cr), and 25% (above ₹5Cr, capped under new regime).

title: Income Tax Slabs under Old Tax Regime (FY 2024-25 / AY 2025-26)
content: Under the Old Tax Regime (optional, requires explicit opt-in at filing), income tax for individuals below 60 years is levied at the following progressive slab rates for FY 2024-25 (AY 2025-26): (1) Up to ₹2,50,000 — Nil (0%); (2) ₹2,50,001 to ₹5,00,000 — 5%; (3) ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 — 20%; (4) Above ₹10,00,000 — 30%. For senior citizens (60–80 years): basic exemption is ₹3,00,000. For super senior citizens (above 80 years): basic exemption is ₹5,00,000. The old regime allows deductions under Chapter VI-A: Section 80C (up to ₹1.5 Lakhs for LIC, ELSS, PPF, home loan principal), Section 80D (health insurance premiums up to ₹25,000/₹50,000), HRA exemption, LTA, standard deduction of ₹50,000 for salaried, and business expenses for self-employed/freelancers. A Section 87A rebate of up to ₹12,500 is available if net taxable income (after all deductions) does not exceed ₹5,00,000. A 4% Health and Education Cess applies on the computed tax. Surcharge at 10% (₹50L–₹1Cr), 15% (₹1Cr–₹2Cr), 25% (₹2Cr–₹5Cr), and 37% (above ₹5Cr) under the old regime.

title: Section 87A Tax Rebate for Low-Income Gig Workers & Freelancers
content: Section 87A of the Income Tax Act provides a direct rebate against computed income tax liability for resident individuals: (A) Under the New Tax Regime (Section 115BAC): Rebate of up to ₹25,000 is available if gross total income does not exceed ₹7,00,000. This effectively makes the total tax payable zero for incomes up to ₹7 Lakhs under the new regime. (B) Under the Old Tax Regime: Rebate of up to ₹12,500 is available if net taxable income (after all deductions) does not exceed ₹5,00,000. This makes effective tax zero for incomes up to ₹5 Lakhs under the old regime. The rebate is applied before adding Health and Education Cess. Gig workers and freelancers with modest annual earnings should note that after legitimate business expense deductions (fuel, tools, subscriptions, subcontracting), their net taxable income may fall within these rebate thresholds, resulting in zero tax liability despite having gross earnings above the basic exemption limit.
